opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to think about a benchmark is in terms of its life cycle. When a benchmark first comes out, it's often really valuable precisely because current models do poorly on it. If you're at, say, ten or twenty percent, there's a lot of signal there: it tells you there's some capability the models are genuinely missing, and it gives you a way to measure whether the ideas you're trying actually help. That's the sweet spot, when there's real headroom and the tasks reflect something you care about.

Then over time, as people work on it, scores climb, and once you're up in the high eighties or nineties, the benchmark becomes much less useful for steering research. You're often fighting over a handful of examples that might be ambiguous or even mislabeled, and the differences between models are as much noise as anything else. At that point it's more of a sanity check than a guide.

The other big thing I look at is contamination and leakage. Public benchmarks are, by definition, out on the web, so there's a real risk that the test data, or close paraphrases of it, end up in training corpora. Then you're not measuring generalization anymore, you're measuring memorization. So we care a lot about having held-out evaluations internally, things that have never been published, so we can check whether improvements on a public benchmark actually transfer to fresh problems.

And then the last question is just: does this benchmark correlate with what users actually experience? Some benchmarks are well-constructed but measure a fairly narrow skill, and you can overfit to them in ways that don't make the model more useful. The ones I find most valuable are those where progress on the benchmark tends to track real improvements, whether that's in coding, reasoning, long-context understanding, or multimodal tasks, so that hill-climbing on it is actually pushing the model in a direction people care about.

So, in short: headroom, freedom from contamination, and alignment with real-world capability. If a benchmark has those three, it's a really useful tool. Once it loses one or more of them, you should probably start looking for the next one.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks are especially valuable when models score around ten or twenty percent, because they reveal missing capabilities and help measure improvement.

r002.rationale: It says a benchmark becomes much less useful for guiding research once scores reach the high eighties or nineties, including roughly 95%, due to noisy differences and a few ambiguous examples.

r003.rationale: It identifies the risk that public test data or close paraphrases enter training corpora, making scores reflect memorization rather than generalization.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a benchmark is useful for about as long as it has headroom and as long as the thing it measures is actually the thing you care about. Those two conditions tend to decay at different rates, and you have to watch both.

The headroom question is the obvious one. When a benchmark first comes out, models are at, say, forty or fifty percent, and the gap between a good model and a mediocre one is large and visible. That's when it tells you something. Once everyone is clustered at ninety-five percent, the remaining differences are mostly noise, or label errors in the test set, or small differences in how you format the prompt. At that point it's not guiding development anymore, it's just a checkbox.

The subtler question is validity. A public benchmark, by definition, is something everyone can see, and that means test data leaks into training corpora, sometimes directly and sometimes through derived discussions and paraphrases on the web. We spend a fair amount of effort on decontamination, but you can never be fully sure. So I tend to trust a benchmark more if we also have a private held-out set that correlates with it. If the public number goes up and the private number doesn't move, that's a strong signal you're optimizing the test rather than the capability.

I also ask whether improving on it transfers. For the kinds of models we build, I care about whether a gain shows up in things people actually do: writing code that compiles and passes tests, answering a multi-step question with the right chain of intermediate facts, handling a long document without losing track of it. A benchmark that measures something narrow can still be fine, as long as you treat it as a diagnostic rather than an objective. The trouble starts when a single number becomes the thing the whole team is chasing, because models are very good at finding the shortest path to a number.

So in practice we use a portfolio. Some public ones for comparability with the rest of the field, some internal ones that are harder and that we refresh regularly, and then a lot of human evaluation and real-usage signals that are messier but closer to ground truth. And we try to retire benchmarks gracefully. When something saturates, you say thank you, you stop reporting it as a headline, and you move on to something that still has room to teach you something.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks are most informative when models score around 40–50%, not 10–30%.

r002.rationale: It says that once scores cluster around 95%, the benchmark stops guiding development and mostly becomes a checkbox.

r003.rationale: It identifies public benchmark data and related web discussions or paraphrases entering training corpora as possible sources of leakage.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: does doing better on this benchmark correspond to something we actually want the model to do better? A benchmark can be very easy to measure and still miss the capability you care about.

Then I’d look at the errors. If you can examine the problems the model gets wrong and learn something useful about its limitations, that’s a good sign. The aggregate score is helpful, but understanding why the model fails is often more valuable for improving it.

With public benchmarks, you also have to be careful about whether the evaluation examples have appeared in training data, or whether you’ve made enough decisions around that particular benchmark that you’re effectively optimizing for the test. You want improvements to carry over to fresh examples and real tasks.

And benchmarks have a lifetime. Once models are getting nearly everything right, you need something that exposes the next set of limitations. So I’d treat a benchmark as one diagnostic tool, alongside other evaluations, rather than as a complete definition of progress.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify benchmarks with initial scores around 10–30% as especially useful.

r002.rationale: It says to find a new benchmark when models get nearly everything right, but does not state that returns diminish at roughly 95%.

r003.rationale: It warns that evaluation examples may have appeared in training data, identifying benchmark exposure as a possible reason for high scores.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what does doing better on this benchmark actually tell us? Ideally, it measures a capability we care about, and improvements on it translate into improvements on problems people encounter in practice.

You also want enough headroom to distinguish models, and you want to understand the errors rather than just look at one aggregate number. Are we getting better at reasoning, or are we getting better at recognizing the particular way the questions are phrased?

With public benchmarks, contamination is always a concern. So I’d want to see whether the gains hold up on fresh examples and related tasks. A benchmark can be a useful diagnostic, but once everyone is optimizing against it, you need other ways to check that you’re making real progress.

r001.rationale: The response discusses headroom for distinguishing models but gives no initial score range or says benchmarks at roughly 10–30% are especially useful.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks become less reliable when people optimize against them, but does not state that returns diminish once scores reach roughly 95%.

r003.rationale: It raises contamination as a concern, but does not identify benchmark data or related material in training as a possible cause of high scores.
